name: Compare and Contrast
summary: Examine two or more items and identify similarities and differences through structured multiple-choice questions.

aiGenerability.notes: AI generates comparison prompts and structured MC questions. Best as guided MC rather than open Venn diagram. AI identifies similarities and differences between items and creates plausible distractors.

itemA.description: First item to compare. Contains name and key facts.

facts.description: Array of 3–5 key facts about this item that will be referenced in comparison questions.
Array of 3–5 key facts about this item.

questions.description: Array of comparison/contrast questions (similarities, differences, categorization).

question.description: Comparison question (e.g., 'Which of the following is true of both rivers?', 'What is a key difference between X and Y?').

explanation.description: Explanation of correct answer with references to facts about both items.

ux.mobileNotes: Items A and B displayed side-by-side on wide screens or stacked on narrow screens. Each item shows name and 3–5 bullet-point facts. Questions appear below, one at a time. Answer options are large tappable buttons.

ageAdaptations.8-10: Two concrete, obviously different items (dog vs. cat, rain vs. snow). 2 simple comparison questions (obvious similarities and differences only). 3 answer options. No multi-criteria analysis. Explanation uses simple language and direct comparison.
ageAdaptations.11-13: Two items with moderate similarity (e.g., two rivers, two historical figures, plant vs. animal cell). 2–3 questions testing both obvious and subtle differences. 3 answer options. One question may require simple categorization. Explanation references specific facts from each item.
ageAdaptations.14-16: Two complex items with multiple dimensions of comparison (e.g., political systems, evolutionary adaptations, literary themes). 3–4 questions testing multi-criteria analysis, implicit relationships, and cause-effect. 3–4 answer options. Questions may require synthesis across categories (structure, function, historical context, etc.). Explanation draws connections and may reference broader frameworks.
